channel.title: Spite Frequencies
channel.description: Music made where it wasn't wanted, and songs that kept the score.

item.title: The song that sang a banned name without saying it
item.description:
In 1919 the British exiled Saad Zaghloul, the leader of Egypt's independence movement. Egyptian accounts say the military authorities then made it an offence even to say his name, punishable by prison and the lash.

The answer came from the street-song writers Badīʿ Khayrī and Sayyid Darwīsh: a little ṭaqṭūqa apparently about dates. Zaghlūl is also a variety of date. "O Zaghloul dates, O sweet dates" is a fruit-seller's cry that a whole city could sing while meaning the man.

The voice on the record is Naʿīma al-Miṣriyya, Cairo's "queen of the records", a woman who made around 150 discs. When it was recorded is still argued over: one scholar files her first Mechian session under 1915, which cannot fit a tribute to a man exiled in 1919. Her personal archive is being digitised, and the answer may be in there.

item.title: The only recording of the noise machines
item.description:
Luigi Russolo built intonarumori, "noise-intoners": boxes with cranks and levers that howled, crackled, gurgled and buzzed. His first concert with them, in Milan in 1914, ended in a riot.

The machines themselves are gone. Of everything he wrote for them, only a fragment of one score survives. What does survive is one gramophone disc made with his brother Antonio in 1921: "Corale" and "Serenata", where a fairly ordinary little orchestra is shadowed and interrupted by a roar nobody can quite place. The French national library lists it as Grammofono R6920, issued in 1924.

It is music aimed at an audience, from people who wanted a fight. The Futurists' later closeness to Mussolini belongs in the story too.

item.title: A hymn recorded by the man who wrote the indictment
item.description:
In 1916 Sol Plaatje published Native Life in South Africa, a book-length charge sheet against the Natives' Land Act. On 16 October 1923, in London, he walked into Zonophone's studio and recorded six sides, with Sylvia Colenso at the piano.

One of them, without fanfare on the label, was Enoch Sontonga's "Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika", the first recording of the hymn that became an anthem of liberation. It runs barely a minute. A prayer asking for Africa to be blessed, cut in the capital of the empire that had just shut the door on his delegation.

item.title: Settling a quarrel with a drum
item.description:
In East Greenland, two people with a real grievance could take it to the whole settlement. Each stood with the frame drum and sang mocking songs at the other. The audience laughed, and the laughter was the verdict. It was a grudge given rules, a stage and a judge, and no one had to die.

In 1906 the Danish linguist William Thalbitzer carried a phonograph to Ammassalik, now Tasiilaq. A woman he wrote down as K'iwingatāk' sang a duel song into the horn. It lasts about a minute.

The cylinder survives in Copenhagen and was published on Inuit: 55 Historical Recordings (ULO, Nuuk / Sub Rosa). These are Greenlandic cultural recordings, and any further use is for Greenlandic voices to decide.

item.title: “My name is Gauhar Jaan!”
item.description:
In November 1902 the Gramophone Company set up a makeshift studio in two hotel rooms in Calcutta. The singer who climbed up to the horn was Gauhar Jaan, a courtesan-artist at a time when reformers were trying to legislate her profession out of existence. She sang a khayal in Raag Jogiya, then shouted her own name at the end so no one could mistake whose voice it was.

She went on to record more than 600 songs in some ten languages. She was not supposed to be the voice of a nation's first record. She made herself impossible to forget.

item.title: A samba that mocked the police chief
item.description:
Samba grew up in Rio's Black neighbourhoods, around houses like Tia Ciata's, under constant police pressure. In January 1917 Casa Edison released "Pelo Telefone", credited to Donga and sung by Baiano on Odeon 121322. It was the hit of that year's carnival.

The popular version opens with the police chief phoning to say the fun can go ahead, a dig at police corruption hidden in a party song. A music the police harassed became Brazil's first samba hit, and its first line was a joke at the police's expense.

item.title: A son keeps his father's grudge
item.description:
In Wagner's Götterdämmerung, Hagen sits up all night guarding the hall while everyone else sleeps, turning over a revenge that was his father's before it was his. In 1922 the English bass Robert Radford recorded the scene in English for HMV, as "Hagen meditates revenge".

Grudges are often inherited. This is one of the earliest discs on which you can hear an inherited grievance being sung as a duty, slowly and in the dark.

item.title: Answering a defeat from the year 451
item.description:
Ghevont Alishan's 1850 poem "Bam Porotan" calls Armenians to remember Avarayr, the battle of 451 in which Vartan Mamikonian fell defending the faith. That defeat has been commemorated for fifteen centuries.

In New York on 11 October 1916, with the Armenian Genocide still under way, Torcom Bézazian recorded it for Victor (69102, matrix B-18462). It is a diaspora singer keeping a very old account open, at the worst possible moment.

item.title: The ballad that convicted Robert Ford
item.description:
Robert Ford shot Jesse James in the back for the reward, was pardoned, and never escaped the song. "The dirty little coward that shot Mister Howard" was passed around as a public verdict the courts never delivered.

Bentley Ball recorded it for Columbia (A3085) in 1919, one of the earliest commercial versions. It is a folk court in waltz time, and Ford is still guilty in it.

item.title: A corrido that names the man who sold the bandit
item.description:
Heraclio Bernal was a Sinaloa bandit-rebel betrayed for a reward in 1888. The corrido that followed made sure the betrayal was remembered as clearly as the man.

Trío Nava recorded "Heraclio Bernal" for Columbia in 1921. It is a ballad doing a newspaper's and a court's job at once: who did it, who paid, who sold whom. A transfer survives in UCLA's Frontera Collection of Mexican and Mexican-American recordings.

item.title: Glory to the soldiers who would not shoot
item.description:
In June 1907 winegrowers in the Languedoc rose up against ruin. Soldiers of the 17th infantry regiment, many of them local men, were sent in and refused to fire on their own people. The chansonnier Montéhus wrote "Gloire au 17e" in their honour, and it was sung for decades as a hymn of collective refusal.

The original pre-1926 disc is still being hunted; Montéhus's 1936 remake streams on Phonobase.

item.title: The band whose tapes the radio destroyed
item.description:
On 22 September 1980, the Estonian punk-art band Propeller played at half-time of a football match between Estonian Radio and Estonian TV staff at Kadriorg Stadium. Alarmed by the crowd, officials cancelled the second set. A riot followed and unrest spread through Tallinn. Forty intellectuals then wrote their famous open letter of protest.

The band was made to disband, singer Peeter Volkonski was banned from the stage, and Estonian Radio destroyed its Propeller recordings. But the band had kept its own copies, and in 1995 the 1980 tapes came out as their only album.

item.title: Banned twice, once for a train
item.description:
Pērkons ("Thunder") were banned by the Soviet authorities in 1983. They carried on under an absurd cover name, the Ensemble of the Soviet Latvia Collective Farm.

On 6 July 1985 they played the open-air stage at Ogre. On the train home some teenage fans wrecked two carriages. The band wasn't on the train, but they were banned again anyway, and the fans got show trials, which Juris Podnieks filmed for Is It Easy to Be Young?. Their early home-studio recordings had already gone hand to hand on tape.

item.title: The Workshop for the Restoration of Unfelt Feelings
item.description:
NSRD was a Riga collective of artists, Hardijs Lediņš and Juris Boiko at the core, who made a wonky, home-taped experimental pop that hardly anyone in the Latvian SSR wanted to hear. Albums like Invalīdu tramvajs ("Invalids' Tram", 1983) existed mostly on cassettes and reel-to-reel. Every year they walked the Bolderāja railway line as an art work.

A small archive label on the edge of Riga, Underbed Storage, now puts out their unreleased reels, along with tapes from the old DIY label T.U.M.S.A. Home Rec.

item.title: A prayer under occupation, and the tape that outlived the ban
item.description:
Lūcija Garūta wrote the cantata Dievs, Tava zeme deg! ("God, Thy Land Is Burning!") to words by Andrejs Eglītis while Latvia was being ground between two occupations. At its premiere on 15 March 1944 she played the organ herself, before a packed church and a crowd outside.

A tape of that premiere survives. One account says you can hear the war outside on it. The Soviet regime later suppressed the cantata. It came back by candlelight at the 1990 Song Festival, when the country was singing its way out.

item.title: Thirty songs left in the radio archive
item.description:
In Soviet Estonia, the Estonian Radio studios were almost the only place a musician could record. Velly Joonas recorded about thirty songs there, and nearly all of them stayed in the archive.

One that escaped, decades later, is "Stopp, seisku aeg!" ("Stop! Stall the time!"). She wrote an Estonian lyric to a Frida song and sang it over an amateur band of young Russians from the Lasnamäe district. The Tallinn label Frotee put it out on a 7" in 2015, and has since dug more buried tracks out of the radio archive.

item.title: And Everything That Is Beautiful Is Beautiful
item.description:
In 1987 the painter Artūras "Šlipas" Šlipavičius and the record collector and dealer Artūras "Baras" Barysas started a band in the Vilnius underground. Many of their home tapes existed in a single copy. The name they chose was Ir Visa Tai Kas Yra Gražu Yra Gražu. The name they didn't choose translates as "Kill the close one, before the far one comes and kills you".

That rejected name could stand as the motto of this whole blog.

item.title: Whispers, flutes and a tape almost no one heard
item.description:
Don Campau's Living Archive of underground cassettes has a short entry on Echidna Aukštyn, a Lithuanian ensemble led by Ramūnas Jaras. Their tape from around 1993 is a bizarre mix of creepy whispers, dark instrumental passages, free improvisation, echoing voices, field recordings and flutes.

Two tapes, a name, and a description. This is what most of the world's music looks like once it has slipped out of memory. If you made it, or own it, we would love to hear from you.

item.title: Music on the ribs
item.description:
After the war, huge amounts of music were forbidden in the Soviet Union: jazz, rock'n'roll, émigré singers, tango, prison songs. Bootleggers worked out that discarded hospital X-ray film could take a groove. Cut into a rough disc with a cigarette-burned hole, someone's chest or skull became a record of Elvis or a banned émigré crooner.

They were called "ribs" or "bones". The state switched the medium off by banning the music; the music simply moved onto the X-rays.

item.title: The grandmother of raï, banned from her own country's radio
item.description:
Cheikha Rimitti could not read or write. She learned her trade singing at weddings and in the bars of western Algeria. In 1954 her song "Charrak Gattà" ("Tear, lacerate") went straight at the taboo of virginity and scandalised the pious.

After independence in 1962, the new government denounced her songs as "folklore perverted by colonialism" and banned her from radio and TV. She kept singing at weddings, then in Paris, until two days before her death in 2006.

item.title: Haló: when towns went to war with songs
item.description:
Among the Anlo-Ewe of southeastern Ghana, haló was a war of insult songs between towns and factions: drums, dance, mime, costume and verses composed to wound. Fieldwork found it in about 88% of Anlo-Ewe towns. A local saying holds that being insulted in song is worse than a beating, because the song outlives you.

It was so powerful that Ghana banned it in its 1960 Criminal Code. We haven't yet found a recording, and the songs still name families. If you know of one, write to us.

item.title: The first song a British court punished someone for performing
item.description:
In August 2018 the Metropolitan Police obtained a gang injunction that barred the drill duo Skengdo x AM from performing certain music. In December they performed their song "Attempted 1.0" at a concert in Camden. In January 2019 a court gave them nine months each, suspended for two years. It was widely called the first prison sentence in British history for performing a song.

The injunction was lifted in 2021. Whatever one thinks of the lyrics, it is a modern case of a state deciding a song is a weapon, like the ban on Zaghloul's name in 1919.

item.title: The song a poll said nobody wants
item.description:
The artists Komar and Melamid and the composer Dave Soldier asked about 500 visitors to the Dia Center's website what they least wanted to hear in music. The answers included bagpipes, accordion, cowboy music, opera, rap, tuba, drum machines, advertising jingles and children's voices.

Then they put all of it into one 22-minute piece, with a children's choir urging you to shop at Walmart. It is a song engineered to be unbearable, and it is a lot of fun.

item.title: The teenage tape you hear on hold
item.description:
In 1989 Tim Carleton and Darrick Deel, both about sixteen, recorded a smooth little instrumental on a four-track in a garage. It ended up as the default hold music on Cisco phone systems, and so it has been played to millions of people who never chose to hear it, while they waited.

A home-made tune became the world's most unwanted repeat listen. Carleton says he never handed over the ownership.

item.title: 840 times
item.description:
Erik Satie left behind a single page of slow, unresolved music headed by a note about playing it 840 times in a row. He never published it and never played it.

On 9–10 September 1963 John Cage took the note at its word. At the Pocket Theatre in Manhattan a relay of pianists, among them John Cale, played it for 18 hours and 40 minutes. Ticket holders got a refund of a nickel for every 20 minutes they stayed.

item.title: Mary Bolton's song
item.description:
For most of the twentieth century, magazines carried small ads: send us your poem and we'll make it a record. Thousands of ordinary people paid. Session musicians set the lyrics in an afternoon, a few copies were pressed, and the record usually went nowhere except the customer's front room.

MSR 851 is one of these: "My Husband, Lover, Friend", sung by "Bobbi Blake" to words by Mary Bolton. It is a stranger's own words, paid into existence and then ignored. The American Song-Poem Music Archives keeps these discs listenable.

item.title: Rough music: when a village plays you out of town
item.description:
Across Europe there was a custom with many names: charivari, cencerrada, scampanata, Katzenmusik, rough music. When a community judged that someone had broken its rules, it gathered at night outside their door and made the worst noise it could: cowbells, pans, horns, whistles. Often the target was a widow or widower who had remarried. The noise was the sentence.

A Spanish cencerrada was taped in Salamanca in 1984 and sits in the Fundación Joaquín Díaz archive. The same habit of banging pans returned as political protest in the 2011 caceroladas.

item.title: A congresswoman at the piano
item.description:
Malinda Jackson Parker was a former member of Liberia's House of Representatives who sat at the piano and half-sang, half-spoke her own songs: odes, praise songs, and a song about a mosquito. The Liberian Landmark Joy came out around 1971 and has been rediscovered abroad as "outsider music".

We would rather hear how she was heard at home: as a singular, self-made voice, and a woman's, in a style nobody else used.

item.title: A guitar built from an oil can
item.description:
Wesseh "Weesay" Freeman lost his sight as a child and taught himself guitar to support his family. He built his own instruments from an oil can, a neck carved with a machete and strings made from bicycle cables. He played the streets of Monrovia for about four dollars a day, until a 2016 video of him playing went around the world.

He died in 2018. The guitar was made from things other people had thrown away, and that is part of why we wanted him here.

item.title: Gnawa master meets a drummer who will not stop
item.description:
Maâlem Mahmoud Gania of Essaouira was the best-known Gnawa musician of his time. On a pair of Voix de Casablanca cassettes (VDC 53 and VDC 51), his guimbri and the clattering qraqeb are joined by an anonymous trap drummer who rolls, crashes and punctuates without a break.

The Moroccan Tape Stash blog called it one of the wildest tapes in its collection. The j-card names only "The Gnawi Mahmoud Guinia". Nobody knows who the drummer was.

item.title: 222 cassettes of Japanese weirdness
item.description:
In the 1980s a small circle around the composer K. Yoshimatsu and his associate Tadashi Kamada ran DD. Records. Over five years they released exactly 222 cassettes: ambient, abstract punk, musique concrète and fragile songs, each with typewritten notes and Xerox covers made from found material.

The original tapes are now collectors' dreams. A 2024 retrospective, Fossil Cocoon, finally made them easy to hear.

item.title: Nine cassettes from a Cape Town cellar
item.description:
In 1986 a 25-year-old radio reporter, Nigel Wrench, recorded South Africa in the most brutal years of late apartheid. His cassettes ended up in the archive of Turnstyle News, in a Cape Town cellar, and stayed there for decades.

Edited from nine of those tapes, ZA86 came out on the 25th anniversary of Mandela's release. Among the street sound and interviews is a Band Aid-style pop song released by the apartheid regime itself, the state trying to sing its own way out.

item.title: Fifty copies and twenty years
item.description:
Yaw Atta-Owusu, as Ata Kak, recorded Obaa Sima in Toronto: Ghanaian highlife sped into home-made rap and drum machines. He pressed about fifty cassettes, sold a few in Ghana, and moved on with his life.

In 2002 a student found one of the tapes in a Ghanaian market stall. It took Awesome Tapes From Africa years to track him down. The 2015 reissue made a record nobody had wanted into one people won't stop playing.

item.title: Forty grimy cassettes behind the halal counter
item.description:
Gary Sullivan's Bodega Pop collects music ripped from cassettes and CDs found in immigrant-run corner shops. On one visit to a halal butcher's in Astoria he came away with some forty grime-encrusted tapes from Algeria, Egypt, Iraq, Lebanon, Morocco, Saudi Arabia, Syria, Turkey and the Emirates.

Most are commercial tapes nobody outside a diaspora shop would ever see. Some are wedding bands with no names on the j-card, and those are the ones we want.

item.title: “Vengeance at Last” — Saint-Saëns, *Samson et Dalila* (1908)
item.description:
Background: This is a strong early recording of an explicit revenge aria. Victor issued “Vengeance at Last” from Samson and Delilah, with baritone Emilio de Gogorza and contralto Louise Homer, accompanied by orchestra. The aria's original French incipit is “À moi l'honneur de la vengeance” (“The honour of vengeance is mine”); a contemporary Victor catalogue advertised the selection in English, so the actual recorded text should be checked against the digitized sound rather than inferred from the French libretto.

Why it fits / decision: Do not describe Delilah as merely “betraying Samson” without retaining the High Priest's role and the political conflict in the scene. The exact recorded excerpt and English translation must be verified from the sound.

item.title: Enrico Caruso — “Vesti la giubba” (1904)
item.description:
Background: The Library of Congress catalog record identifies the recording date as 1 February 1904, label Victor, catalog 930, matrix B-1002, take 1, and recording location New York. The record's issue/publication date is not separately displayed in the metadata retrieved here. The 1904 catalog number and period discographies support an early issue, but the release date still needs confirmation from a contemporary Victor catalog or trade advertisement before this candidate is marked fully verified.

Candidate id: GM-IT-001

Performer: Enrico Caruso, tenor

Title: “Vesti la giubba” (also catalogued as I pagliacci / Pagliacci. Vesti la giubba)

Original language: Italian

Genre: Opera aria; from Pagliacci

Recording date: 1904-02-01 (Library of Congress National Jukebox item metadata)

Recording location: New York, New York

Why it fits / decision: Retain as a strong PARTIALLY VERIFIED candidate for a mix concerned with betrayal, grief, and the performance of composure after injury. It is not a “revenge” track in isolation. The 1904 LOC master is preferable to Caruso's later 1907 orchestral re-recording for this project because its metadata is explicit and it predates the cutoff by more than two decades. It still requires publication-date and rights/transfer confirmation before commercial use.

item.title: “Sì, vendetta” — Verdi, *Rigoletto* (Vocalion, ca. 1921)
item.description:
Background: The Act III duet “Sì, vendetta” (“Yes, vengeance”) from Verdi's Rigoletto is an explicit operatic statement of revenge. Florida Atlantic University's Recorded Sound Archives (FAU RSA) has a digitized 78rpm item titled “Don Giovanni - La ci darem; Rigoletto - Si vendetta (Yes, My Vengeance),” with the second track attributed to Verdi. The archive item identifies catalogue number 60019, performers Evelyn Scotney and Giacomo Rimini, 78 rpm, 10-inch.

Why it fits / decision: Avoid collapsing Gilda's and Rigoletto's motives into one. The dramatic text and actual recording should be consulted before describing who sings each phrase and how the performance frames their agency.

item.title: “Revenge! Timotheus Cries” — Handel, *Alexander's Feast* (Vocalion X-9560, 1924/25)
item.description:
Background: This is a particularly strong example of music represented as an instrument of retaliation. In Handel's Alexander's Feast, the singer Timotheus evokes the Furies and the ghosts of Greeks slain in earlier wars with Persia. His song moves Alexander toward burning Persepolis, framed by the poem as vengeance for Greek dead. The aria is not simply an aggressive title: the libretto explicitly stages a remembered injury, summoned dead, and a retaliatory act. It is a fictionalized ancient-historical narrative mediated through John Dryden's 1697 ode and Newburgh Hamilton's adaptation, not a neutral record of Alexander's actual motives.

Performer: Malcolm McEachern, bass; Aeolian Orchestra.

Label/catalogue: Vocalion X-9560, 10-inch 78rpm, issued in the United Kingdom.

Session/matrix: specialist Vocalion sessionography lists London, October 1924?, matrix/session numbers 03724 and 03725, with “Revenge Timotheus cries” parts 1 and 3 and “Behold a ghastly band” part 2; issue X-9560 is linked to 03724 and …

Publication: the UK Vocalion catalogue's 1926 edition (covering issues through November 1925) lists X-9560 as “Revenge! Timotheus Cries,” Alexander's Feast (Handel), parts I and II, with Aeolian Orchestra, bass Malcolm McEachern; its foreword says …

Cross-check: a later McEachern discography independently lists X-9560 and matrices/issues 03724/03725. A 2010 specialist review says McEachern recorded the aria on Vocalion in the early 1920s and comments on the 1924 studio circumstances; useful …

item.title: Shoqnia e hengxhive e shahirave, «Kanga e Oso Kukës» (Gramophone 10771; matrix 4570r; Shkodër, 1908)
item.description: Background: A 2023 Albanian-language cultural article published by the Albanian Ministry of Defence describes a song about Oso Kuka, attributing its composition to Zenel Maha and dating its creation to the time of the 1862 Vranina battle. It says the song comprised 22 stanzas and was first performed by a Shkodër aheng ensemble in a local coffeehouse. The account presents Oso Kuka's stand against Montenegrin forces as a narrative of resistance and refusal to surrender. A scholarly study of Gjergj Fishta's Lahuta e Malcis independently situates the five-canto Oso Kuka cycle in 1862 and identifies it as a central episode of the Albanian national epic.

item.title: (lead) — Helen Paul, “Tzain ma Hunchetz” (Columbia, April 1918 session)
item.description:
Background: The museum identifies the song as an ode to the earliest organized Armenian revolutionary groups, especially the Protectors of the Fatherland (Bashdban Hayrenyat's), an organization associated with Erzerum. The composition is attributed to an unknown writer and is believed to date from the late nineteenth century.

Proposed role: Revolutionary memory / collective resistance / historical grievance

Why it fits / decision: The song is a historical ode to revolutionary organizers and can fit collective resistance / revolutionary memory. It may carry an underlying grievance against Ottoman repression, but the exact recorded text has not yet been transcribed or examined. Do not assign a specific retaliatory narrative, event or political factional programme without further evidence.

item.title: Mardiros Der Sarkis Tashjian, “Hairenikt Mortsir” (Columbia E531/4084, 1909)
item.description:
Background: The song stages a confrontation between the emigrant and an unnamed “foreigner” who urges abandonment of the homeland as barren and ruined. The singer's answer is emphatically defiant: he will continue to love and remember Armenia and Cilicia. This makes the recording a strong example of diasporic grievance and resistance to assimilation, although it is not a direct account of a single retaliatory act or a fully documented protest against a named policy.

Proposed role: Diasporic grievance / defiant remembrance / anti-assimilation

item.title: Tashjian Brothers, “Himi El Lrenk” (Columbia E668/4953, 1910)
item.description:
Background: The Armenian Museum identifies “Himi El Lrenk” as one of the 28 songs recorded by the Tashjian Brothers in 1910 and reproduces the Columbia E668/4953 label. The museum does not publish a full transcription of this particular 1910 performance.

Proposed role: Collective protest / anti-subjugation / refusal of silence / armed resistance rhetoric

Why it fits / decision: This is an exceptionally strong song-family match for the project's core: collective grievance, accusation of oppression, forced displacement, chains, loss of arms and land, attacks on religious/cultural institutions, refusal of silence, and explicit call to resistance. It is not merely patriotic praise.

item.title: Mardiros Der Sarkis Tashjian, “Himi El Lrenk” (Columbia E529-4100, 1909)
item.description:
Background: Armenian online songbooks attribute a song under this title to Raphael Patkanian's nineteenth-century poem “The Death of Vardan Mamikonian.” A published song-family text asks whether Armenians should remain silent while their land and arms are taken, chains are forged, and the community is driven from its homeland; it ends by rejecting silence and calling for resistance.

Proposed role: Collective resistance / refusal of silence

item.title: Tashjian Brothers, “Menk Bedk E Grvenk” (Columbia E661 / matrix 4973-1, 1910)
item.description:
Background: The text is unusually explicit about collective loss, unheard grievance, and armed recovery. It directly contrasts passive lament with organized resistance. This is a strong conceptual fit for the project's collective grievance / defiance strand, but it is not necessarily a revenge narrative in the narrow sense.

Proposed role: Collective resistance / armed recovery / anti-subjugation

item.title: Mardiros Tashjian, “Dalvorig” (Columbia, 1909)
item.description:
Background: A pre-1909 English-language text witness is Alice Stone Blackwell's Armenian Poems (Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1896), which includes “The Son of Dalvorig,” attributed to Mihran Damadian, pp. 135–138. The poem's speaker identifies himself as a free son of Dalvorig, refuses to bow before the Turk, calls Armenian brothers to join him for liberty, rejects foreign domination, and describes armed struggle. In its closing movement, the speaker says that for every blow dealt him, he returns a thousand.

Proposed role: Anti-subjugation / armed defiance / collective liberation

Why it fits / decision: Strong fit for anti-subjugation, collective defiance and armed resistance. The text is not a neutral folk outlaw song: it belongs to a specific Armenian political and historical repertoire. The archive should contextualize its revolutionary language, identify the historical actors as carefully as possible, and avoid turning a song-family text into a claim about the exact 1909 performance before transcription.

item.title: Tashjian Brothers, “Tartzial Paylets” (Columbia E658/4964, 1910)
item.description:
Background: Houshamadyan's Armenian-language Sassoun collection publishes a song titled “Դարձեալ փայլեց” (“It Shone Again”) in the Alahaydoyan collection. The text describes a freedom flag raised over Sassoun, calls for aid to the homeland, names Gurgen, Vahan, Hrayr Tzhokhk and Andranik in the mountains of Dalvorik, describes an order from the Sultan's palace to destroy the fedayi positions, and includes the explicit cry “Ժամանակն է վրեժ լուծել” (“It is time to take revenge”). The closing stanza describes gunfire from Armenian positions and enemy casualties.

Proposed role: Collective resistance / retaliation / armed defence

item.title: Tashjian Brothers, “Kerezmanis Togh” (Columbia E657/4955, 1910)
item.description:
Background: Houshamadyan's Sassoun / Alahaydoyan collection preserves a song titled “Sasnou Kavar (Hrayr Tjokhki Hishadagin)” — “Land of Sassoun (In Memory of Hrayr Tzhokhk)”. The text praises Sassoun, names revolutionary figures, describes conflict with Ottoman forces, and includes a speaker threatening to destroy the Ottoman army. Houshamadyan attributes this particular text to an ARF-affiliated family from Shenig in the Moush Valley and cites the ARF Archives in Watertown, Massachusetts. This is valuable regional and community provenance, but it does not establish that these exact verses occur on Columbia E657/4955.

Performer: Tashjian Brothers — Mardiros, Nishan and Levon Der Sarkis.

Title on discography: “Kerezmanis Togh”.

Common/related title: “Hrayr Tzhokhki Yerke” / “Hrayr Tzhokhk’s Song”, according to the Armenian Museum.

Label and issue: Columbia E657/4955.

Session: New York, autumn 1910.

Release: 1911.

Language: Armenian.

item.title: Tashjian Brothers, “Akh Vasburagan” (Columbia E666/4974, 1910)
item.description:
Background: The Armenian-language ERGIR page “ԱԽ ՎԱՍՊՈՒՐԱԿԱՆ” (“Akh Vaspurakan”) attributes the words to S. Jamkochyan. Its stanzas: - mourn Vaspurakan and the Armenian dead; - condemn captivity, foreign dependence and disunity; - call for Armenian unity and explicitly say “Պէտք է մենք լուծենք վրէժ հայկական” — approximately, “We must exact Armenian revenge”; - describe Van and its districts filled with bodies and fields stained with Armenian blood; - denounce the Ottoman army and artillery; - end with a call to take up rifles as Armenian communities and homes are attacked.

Performer: Tashjian Brothers — Mardiros, Nishan and Levon Der Sarkis.

Title: “Akh Vasburagan” (also transliterated “Akh Vaspurakan”).

Label / catalogue: Columbia E666/4974.

Session: New York, autumn 1910.

Release: 1911.

Paired side: “Zartir Vortiag” (Columbia E666/4975).

Language: Armenian.

item.title: Zabelle Panosian, “Khavarel Yem” (Columbia E4010, June 1918)
item.description:
Background: The Canary Records title gloss is “I Am Darkened.” Armenian lexical sources confirm that խաւարել / խավարել can mean to darken, become gloomy, or be overwhelmed by sorrow, but this is only a lexical clue, not a translation of the song. The Panosian project includes translated song texts and historical notes, but the full lyric of this item has not yet been independently checked in this research pass.

Performer: Zabelle Panosian, soprano, with orchestra.

Title: “Khavarel Yem” (publisher's English gloss: “I Am Darkened”).

Original label / catalogue: Columbia E4010.

Matrix / take: 84458-1 is listed for “Khavarel Yem” in the Columbia E-Series discography. Canary Records' later digital reissue contains two performances labelled take 1 (2:49) and take 2 (3:18); do not assume take 2 is the same matrix or issue without …

Recording date/location: June 1918, New York, per Columbia E-Series discography and the Armenian Mirror-Spectator's reproduction of the original Columbia label.

Issue: Columbia E4010; the Mirror-Spectator identifies the original record and dates it June 1918.

Exact later access copy: Canary Records, I Am Servant of Your Voice: March 1917–June 1918, digital album. Bandcamp lists “Khavarel Yem (I Am Darkened) take 1” (track 8, 2:49) and take 2 (track 13, 3:18), with streaming and high-quality MP3/FLAC …

item.title: Tashjian Brothers, “Tashnagtsagan Khump” (Columbia E665-4962, 1910)
item.description: Background: A useful later Armenian-language text witness appears in Armenian National Songs, second edition (Armenian Youth Federation of America, 1962), contents p. 1 and song text/commentary around pp. 7–8 (PDF pages/printed pagination should be checked against the physical edition). It includes a song titled “Dashnagtsagan Khoumb” and describes the song as telling of Armenian Revolutionary Federation fedayi bands fighting in Sassoun under Antranik's leadership.

item.title: Sayyid Darwīsh, “Istaʿgibū yā Afandiyya” (1914-listed; 78 rpm issue unresolved)
item.description:
Background: This is a particularly valuable non-Anglophone lead because the text itself—not just the title—describes an economic grievance: kerosene price inflation, black-market selling, shortages, and the presence of police officials. It may fit collective grievance and accusation better than revenge or personal retaliation. It also records a specific urban experience of scarcity and price exploitation around the First World War.

Proposed role: Economic grievance / public accusation / social protest

item.title: Sayyid Darwīsh, “Qum yā Miṣrī” (Odeon; 1919 work, specific disc date unknown)
item.description:
Background: The work is a strong collective defiance / anticolonial solidarity lead. It is not simply a generic patriotic song: it emerged in the 1919 uprising and uses an imperative call to collective action. The solidarity stanza is particularly important because it can be read as an explicit appeal across religious communities; verify its presence in the actual Odeon issue rather than importing it from a later printed lyric.

Proposed role: Anticolonial defiance / collective grievance / solidarity

item.title: María García, “La noche de Reyes” (Asturias; recorded 19 January 1939)
item.description:
Background: The documented plot is a killing in response to an alleged sexual betrayal. Before classifying the work as revenge, distinguish: - the father's narrated motive; - the child's position as listener; - the ballad's narrative stance; - the performer's own stance, which is not established by the catalogue.

Proposed role: domestic violence, accusation and retaliatory killing in an Asturian ballad

Why it fits / decision: A strong, exact, publicly catalogued revenge-ballad recording, but not eligible for the pre-1926 core. Its value is as a post-cutoff comparison and as a pointer toward earlier Iberian ballad witnesses. No listening or transcription was performed in this pass.

item.title: Roland C. Nathaniels, “Anlo Patriotic Song” / “Ewe Battle Hymn” (Zonophone 3972, 1925)
item.description: Background: The titles “Anlo Patriotic Song” and “Ewe Battle Hymn” invite investigation of collective identity, resistance and historical grievance, but neither title proves an anti-colonial message. “Battle hymn” may be a conventional religious or ceremonial description; the discography calls it a “Native melody,” not a political protest song. “Patriotic” may refer to Anlo community identity without a specific grievance or adversary.

item.title: (lead) — Babu Surendra Nath Banerjee, “Bande Mataram and Swadeshi” / “Partition of Bengal” (National Grand Record / Beka, catalogue 20290–20291)
item.description: Background: The Berlin museum's collection record identifies the physical object as a shellac disc, attributes the performance to Babu Surendra Nath Banerjee, and names National Grand Record as maker and publisher. Its title is “Speech on ‘Bande Mataram and Swadeshi’”.

item.title: (lead) — Rabindranath Tagore, “Bande Mataram” (H. Bose cylinder / Pathé-H. Bose disc; 1890s–1908, date disputed)
item.description:
Background: “Bande Mataram” became a major song of the Swadeshi movement and resistance to the 1905 partition of Bengal. Its circulation was entangled with political meetings, anti-colonial mobilisation, police searches and destruction/confiscation of nationalist recording material. The gramophone/cylinder was not simply a neutral imported technology: local entrepreneurs and activists used it to circulate political sound.

Proposed role: Collective grievance / anticolonial defiance / protest

item.title: 吉田奈良丸, “矢頭右衛門の誠忠” (Victor catalogue, 1915)
item.link: https://sloev.github.io/grudgemusic-public/posts/gm-jp-001-吉田奈良丸-矢頭右衛門の誠忠-victor-catalogue-1915/
item.guid: https://sloev.github.io/grudgemusic-public/posts/gm-jp-001-吉田奈良丸-矢頭右衛門の誠忠-victor-catalogue-1915/
item.description: Background: A 2015 Kobecco historical feature places 矢頭右衛門七 in the Ako-retainer revenge tradition: his father joined the revenge pledge, and the son is represented as taking up the cause after his father's death. This is useful secondary narrative context for the title’s “loyal fidelity” framing, but it does not establish the exact text performed on these four sides.

item.title: 吉田奈良丸, “勝田新左エ門” (Victor 50181–50182; catalogue year 1915)
item.description: Background: Kotobank's entry in the Nihon Daihyakka Zensho identifies 勝田新左衛門武堯 (Katsuta Shinzaemon Taketaka, 1680–1703) as an Akō retainer and one of the forty-seven rōnin who attacked Kira's residence on 14 December 1702 and were ordered to commit seppuku on 4 February 1703. This establishes that the named person belongs to the Akō vendetta tradition; it is not proof that the recording narrates the raid, nor that it expresses the same moral interpretation as later Chūshingura works.

item.title: “Ignacio Parra” (parts 1–2), Rafael Herrera Robinson, Edison two-minute cylinders (1904)
item.description: Background: The Frontera Collection’s 2017 specialist history describes “Ignacio Parra” and “Heraclio Bernal” as early corridos about rebels active in the late 1880s during the Díaz dictatorship. It reports that Herrera later re-recorded many early cylinder titles for Victor and Columbia but did not reprise these two rebel ballads; the article relays corrido scholar James Nicolopulos’s interpretation that political pressure and a “seditious undercurrent” explain the omission. This supports a probable defiance/resistance connection and justifies a research lead.

item.title: Valentín Mancera corrido family (Victor 97040 / Victor 72590-A, 1905–c.1920)
item.description: Background: The printed corrido family tells of Valentín Mancera, a Guanajuato bandit whose lover and her sister betray him for money, leading to capture and execution. The 2016 analysis treats the song as an accusatory, didactic narrative about betrayal and punishment. That is within the project's grievance/punishment remit. The link from that narrative to the exact wording of each early recording remains incomplete, so this stays at C level.

item.title: Smyrnaiki Estudiantina, “Marche de Niyazi et Enver Bey / Marche Huriet” (Odeon 58588, June 1908)
item.description:
Background: The Kounadis record page publishes Turkish lyrics and an English translation. The text includes the lines:

Proposed role: Anti-despotism / collective grievance / revolutionary liberation

Why it fits / decision: This is a clear anti-despotism / liberation text associated with the 1908 Young Turk Revolution and the restoration of constitutional government. Its explicit references to the oppressed, informers, despotism, freedom and bondage make the grievance/protest content textual rather than inferred from the title.

item.title: Nubar Effendi, “Vatan Canto” (Odeon 54584, 1908–1909)
item.description:
Background: The archive publishes Turkish lyrics and an English translation. The refrain reads:

Proposed role: Constitutional-revolution context / freedom-and-equality rhetoric

Why it fits / decision: The recording is dated 1908–1909 in Constantinople and celebrates the constitutional-era language of freedom, justice, equality and nation. It belongs alongside the 1908 “Marche Huriet” as evidence of the musical rhetoric circulating around the Young Turk / constitutional revolution.

item.title: Jacob Algava, “Hermanos mis queridos” (Gramophone, March 1909)
item.description: Background: The Hebrew University publication identifies the song as a Judeo-Spanish adaptation / abridgement of Joseph Pinto's “Cante nuevo por la constitución,” published in the Istanbul Judeo-Spanish periodical El Djugueton on 10 November 1908 and sung to the melody of the Turkish song “Yaşasın Hürriyet adalet” (“Long live freedom, justice”). It links the song to the reinstatement of the 1876 Ottoman Constitution in 1908 after the Young Turk revolt.

item.title: Çakum Effendi, “Malandanzas del asker” (Gramophone 11-12734, 1911)
item.description: Background: The Hebrew University scholarly commentary identifies this as one of the Ladino songs about “askerlik” — military service imposed on Jews by Ottoman authorities from 1908. It notes that Çakum's version is close to Haim Effendi's earlier / parallel recorded version and that rare oral-tradition versions probably derive from these commercial recordings.

item.title: Mlle Mariette, “El sentenciado del bajá” (Zonophone X-103831, 1911)
item.description: Background: The Hebrew University / Jewish Music Research Centre commentary identifies this as a truncated version of the Sephardic romance “El sentenciado del bajá” (CMP H23), known in only a few printed and recorded sources in longer versions. It explains that the protagonist is sentenced to death after refusing the advances of an anonymous “Turk”; in some versions the protagonist is female, in others male. The fuller romance develops into a dialogue with the protagonist's mother, who is asked to save the condemned child but cannot help. The commentary explicitly notes that this dialogue is missing from Mlle Mariette's recording.

item.title: “You Ought to Be Arrested and Put in Jail” — Land Norris, Okeh 40374 (1924)
item.description: Background: A useful lead emerged from comparing the title with early song-family references:

item.title: Bascom Lamar Lunsford — “Jesse James” (Okeh 40155, 1924)
item.description: Background: The traditional “Jesse James” ballad frames Robert Ford's killing of James as betrayal by a trusted associate and repeatedly condemns Ford as a coward. It can therefore serve as a public accusation/counter-insult and betrayal-grievance text. It is not straightforward revenge: the familiar text condemns the killing but does not narrate a retaliatory act against Ford. Later folklore and popular culture sometimes append or associate revenge for James's death with Edward O'Kelly, but that is not evidence that this particular 1924 performance does so.

item.title: Riley Puckett — “Jesse James” (Columbia 15033-D, 1925)
item.description: Background: This is the familiar “Jesse James” ballad family (Laws E1), not the separate, more historically critical “Jesse James II” song sometimes also recorded under that title. The common ballad condemns Robert Ford as a “dirty little coward” for killing James after gaining his trust. That makes the song a possible case of betrayal accusation and counter-insult, rather than a direct narrative of revenge carried out.

item.title: Ford and Ford — “Skeeg-A-Lee Blues” (Paramount 12244-A, 1924)
item.description: Background: The 2023 Social History of American Music chapter calls the Ford and Ford recording the first vocal version of Stagger Lee. Patrick Blackman's 2013 Sing Out! Stagolee compendium explicitly disputes the connection: he includes the recording among early examples but says the Ford and Ford track is hard to connect to the Stagolee narrative. The compendium identifies Ma Rainey's late-1925 recording, issued in 1926, as the first version with clearly recognizable Stagolee lines. This is a real scholarly/editorial disagreement, not a resolved lyric match. No authenticated lyric sheet or transcription tied to matrix 1899-2 was located.

item.title: Furry Lewis — “Billy Lyons and Stack O'Lee” (Vocalion 1132, 1927)
item.description: Background: The title explicitly names Billy Lyons and Stack O'Lee, the two figures at the centre of the Stagger Lee ballad cycle. This is a strong research lead for a song about retaliatory violence, but the exact lyric and moral point of view must be established from this performance. Later summaries and familiar lyrics are not substitutes for the 1927 master.

item.title: Long “Cleve” Reed and Little Harvey Hull — “Original Stack O'Lee Blues” (Black Patti 8030, 1927)
item.description: Background: This is an early, distinct vocal interpretation of the Stagger Lee / Stack O'Lee murder-ballad family. It is highly relevant to research on retaliatory violence and outlaw memory. However, its exact lyric, narrative sequence and stance toward the killing must be checked against the recording; do not substitute later lyrics or assume the title alone establishes a revenge motive.

item.title: Riley Puckett, “The Boston Burglar” (Columbia 15050-D, 1925)
item.description:
Background: “The Boston Burglar” belongs to a broadside-derived family related to “Botany Bay.” The narrative commonly follows a young man who turns to crime, is caught and sentenced, and warns listeners against lawbreaking. A contemporary traditional-song account explains the warning and penal-transportation narrative: https://clarelibraries.ie/localstudies/music-and-literature/music/collections/traditional-music-sessions-from-clare-live/the-carroll-mackenzie-music-collection/singers-and-songs-of-county-clare-from-the-carroll-mackenzie-collection/songs-of-clare-the-boston-burglar-sung-by-pat-macnamara/ . The Ballad Index groups “Boston Burglar” texts under Laws L16 and notes the overlap with “Botany …

Proposed role: Penal sanction / cautionary ballad; adjacent to the core grievance programme

item.title: Al Craver [Vernon Dalhart], “Naomi Wise” (Columbia 15053-D, 1925)
item.description:
Background: The Naomi Wise ballad tradition concerns the murder of a young woman by a man who had promised marriage. Delia Dattilo traces the story's nineteenth-century printed and oral forms, notes the historical case's uncertain details, and distinguishes versions that do and do not include the killer's capture, confession or punishment. The article identifies the 1925 Columbia 15053-D recording as a Carson Robison song related to West Virginia oral culture, with a tune and lyrics different from the older Craven-derived “Song of Naomi Wise” text.

Proposed role: Accusation / murder-ballad justice narrative; conditional

item.title: Al Craver [Vernon Dalhart], “Sentenced to Life Behind These Grey Walls” (Columbia 15060-D, 1925)
item.description:
Background: The full Columbia title explicitly frames the subject as a life sentence and confinement. This is a strong title-level punishment lead, but the title alone does not tell us whether the singer accepts the sentence, protests wrongful conviction, laments separation, or speaks in another dramatic register. No verified lyric transcription has yet been found for matrix W141311.

Proposed role: Penal sentence / possible grievance testimony

item.title: George Reneau, “Woman's Suffrage” (Vocalion 14999, 1925)
item.description:
Background: The title identifies the political issue, not the singer's stance. The performance could be advocacy, ridicule, anti-suffrage satire, comic role-play, or something more ambivalent. Do not infer opposition from the performer, genre, title or the era's gender politics. Do not classify this as protest, grievance or counter-protest until the actual lyrics and performance are inspected.

Proposed role: Political protest / anti-suffrage satire / gender grievance (undetermined)

item.title: Roba Stanley & Bill Patterson, “Little Frankie” (Okeh 40436, matrix 8848; recorded December 1924)
item.description:
Background: This is more than a title-only association. The LOC finding aid preserves the opening narrative and the lover's wrongdoing; Wolfe's account identifies the performance as a female-voiced version of “Frankie and Johnnie” in which Frankie kills Alvin, is tried and acquitted. The song therefore represents retaliation for perceived romantic betrayal, with a woman as the retaliating protagonist. It is a narrative representation, not evidence of the singer's own experience or endorsement.

Proposed role: revenge / retaliatory murder ballad, female-voiced Frankie variant

item.title: Julius Sutton, “Single Girl” (Gordon cylinder A79, Item NC117; 28 October 1925)
item.description:
Background: The recorded text opens by warning young women against marriage. It contrasts the singer's former freedom and decent clothing with the labour and deprivation of married life, then describes a husband returning with a bottle and wishing she were dead, followed by children crying for food. The singer repeatedly wishes she were single again.

Why it fits / decision: Add as GM-US-018, B — probable core candidate. The exact recording and pre-cutoff fixation date are directly documented, and the text supplies a clear grievance/defiance mechanism. Do not describe it as revenge; its value is a recorded account of domestic harm and a warning against marriage.

item.title: Papus Rache / Bar Kochba (Yiddish theatre repertory)
item.description:
Background: A German-language discography compilation titled Zusammenstellung der Schallplatten mit Themen aus dem Orient lists a recording under the work heading Bar Kochba (Goldfaden):

Why it fits / decision: This classification is based on the work's explicit plot function and the named aria. It should not be upgraded to a historical example of Jewish-Roman retaliation or a record of collective grievance without analysis of the libretto. The wider operetta draws on the Bar Kokhba revolt and later Jewish national memory, but its plot is a nineteenth-century theatrical construction.

item.title: Egypt: Dinshaway mawwal / ballad tradition (1906)
item.description:
Background: Ziad Fahmy's study Ordinary Egyptians: Creating the Modern Nation through Popular Culture describes the near-immediate commemoration of the 1906 Dinshaway incident in rural colloquial Egyptian mawāwīl (singular mawwāl, ballad-like sung narratives). The book reports that these songs circulated widely in the countryside and that many were probably not composed by a single identifiable writer. One mawwāl is attributed to Sheikh Mustafa ʿAjāj.

Why it fits / decision: The reported ballad appears to imagine retaliatory humiliation or punishment of the colonial authority as a response to an injury understood as dishonouring. It may be closer to retaliatory justice or collective vengeance than to a private, calculated grudge. The exact wording and narrative sequence must be checked against Kamal's Arabic transcript before fixing the taxonomy.

item.title: Bengal's early recorded *Bande Mataram* cluster (1905–1908)
item.description: Background: The National Institute of Science Communication / Indian Journal of History of Science article by Suvobrata Sarkar gives unusually useful recording-industry evidence. It says Hemendramohan Bose founded his phonographic business in 1905; in early 1906, at the height of anti-partition agitation, H. Bose's first batch of cylinder records was offered for sale, comprising patriotic songs sung by Rabindranath Tagore, Dwijendralal Roy and others. Bose later partnered with Pathé to transfer some cylinders to discs. One Pathé–H. Bose record has Tagore's recitation of Sonār Tarī on one side and Bande Mataram on the other; Sarkar identifies it as the oldest existing voice recording of Tagore. …

item.title: Japan lead: Yoshida Naramaru, *Akō Gishi-den Toiri* (Royal Record)
item.description:
Background: Nichibunken’s Rōkyoku SP Record Digital Archive describes a collection of 9,998 SP records donated by collector Morikawa Tsukasa in 2014. Its public database includes label images for all digitized records, but sound is publicly available only when copyright protection has expired; otherwise audio is restricted to on-site access. The current archive overview reports 2,237 audio titles and 5,534 label-image titles (as of February 2023). The Toiri record's presence in the 2016 institutional prospectus establishes a Nichibunken holding, but its inclusion in the online searchable subset and its audio status still need item-level confirmation.

Why it fits / decision: The title points to the raid by the Akō retainers, the climactic collective act of vengeance in the Chūshingura narrative. This is a strong thematic lead for collective revenge / retaliatory justice in dramatic-historical storytelling, not evidence that the recorded performance recounts the historical raid accurately. The 47 retainers’ revenge story is a cultural narrative with a long and shifting performance history; do not collapse the fictionalized stage/folk narrative, later national memory, and the historical events into one evidentiary category.

item.title: “Dalvorig” / “Dalvorigtsi” — Mihran Damadian; Tashjian Columbia recordings, 1909 and 1910
item.description: Background: The 1962 Armenian National Songs, second edition, includes “Dalvorig” and prints the following English translation (James G. Mandalian translation, per the volume's introduction): - “Torrents of hail pelted the plain of Khanasor” - “Wreaking revenge, Dashnaktzakan Fedayee” - “The soldiers of Andranik / Are wreaking revenge on the Kurds” - The Mazrig Kurd is described as panic-stricken and being killed by fedayi bullets. - A later stanza states that the Mazrig tribe was wiped out and Khanasor's green was painted red with blood. - Another stanza says the “avenging Armenian brave” does not harm a Kurdish woman's hair.

item.title: “Revenge! Timotheus cries” — Handel, *Alexander’s Feast*
item.description:
Background: The aria is a direct thematic fit: its text explicitly stages revenge and vengeance. It is a literary/classical representation, not evidence of an actual grievance or a contemporary act of revenge.

Why it fits / decision: Keep both recordings in the research queue as LEADS in this research dossier, with HMV D589 / 02927 the first search target. A separate formal candidate record GM-UK-001 and the README crosswalk currently map the Vocalion lead to B — PROBABLE; this is a documented status mismatch, not a fresh promotion in this dossier. Reconcile only after the exact identity/date evidence is reviewed across both records. The performer and matrix take are disputed across discographies and must not be silently resolved. Neither is eligible for a production mix yet because the exact archival audio and rights …

item.title: Helen Paul, “Tzain ma Hunchetz” (Columbia E-4661; 1918)
item.description:
Background: The Armenian Museum of America identifies the piece as the first known recording of an ode to Armenian revolutionaries from Erzurum, especially the Protectors of the Fatherland (Bashdban Hayrenyats). It says the composition was written by an unknown author in the late nineteenth century. The museum describes the record as made in April 1918 and notes that the Nishkian Phonograph Shop in Fresno carried the Columbia disc.

Why it fits / decision: This is potentially one of the strongest early Armenian-American collective-resistance recordings located so far. Its significance is not that it is a revenge song, but that a commercial diaspora disc captured a late-nineteenth-century revolutionary ode in New York in April 1918, just weeks before the declaration of the First Republic of Armenia. It may be suitable for a collective grievance / resistance sequence if the exact recorded lyrics and composition status can be established.

item.title: Kolkata theatre recording lead — “Khune Nahak: Gana Gana Gana” (1902)
item.description: Background: A significant contextual match has now been found: Khun-e-Nahaq (also rendered Khun-e-nahaq, Khoon-e-Nahaq, Khune Nahak) is identified in scholarship as an Urdu adaptation of Hamlet by Munshi Mehdi Hasan Ahsan, staged by the Parsi Alfred Company in 1898. Kathryn Hansen's Stages of Life appendix identifies Ahsan/Mehdi Hasan as the author of Khun-e Nahaq (based on Hamlet); research on Shakespeare reception in India likewise identifies the 1898 Urdu Hamlet adaptation and notes that it was transformed into a musical. This makes revenge a plausible dramatic frame for the play, not yet a demonstrated lyric mechanism in the recorded selection.

item.title: Mardiros Der Sarkis Tashjian — 1909 Columbia Armenian-language recordings
item.description: Background: # Mardiros Der Sarkis Tashjian — 1909 Columbia Armenian-language recordings

item.title: Tashjian Brothers 1910 Columbia repertoire: Dalvorig and Grvetsek Dgherk
item.description:
Background: Houshamadyan's account of the Capuchin college in Mezire (Mamuret-ul-Aziz/Harput region) says that after the 1908 Ottoman constitutional proclamation, the college orchestra played Armenian patriotic songs at public events, including “Pamp Voradan,” “Grvetsek Dgherk” and “Dalvorig.” This establishes that both titles circulated as patriotic repertoire in an Armenian institutional/public setting in the Harput region. It does not establish that the Tashjian recording derives from that exact local performance tradition, nor does it supply lyrics or authorship.

Why it fits / decision: The museum characterizes the 1910 repertoire broadly as patriotic songs, odes to fedayi/freedom fighters and songs of loss. That does not automatically make any title revenge, retaliation or grievance testimony. In particular:

item.title: Candidate research lead: Vahan Boyajian, “Derzor Dasdaanaci” (Bilbil 2)
item.description: Background: Yıldız identifies “Derzor Dasdaanaci” as a popular song with many versions by different singers. She describes it as narrating the long and painful deportation of Armenians to Deir ez-Zor in Syria, and as a lament that symbolically depicts violence committed around 1915. She interprets the song as a site of memory and “postmemory,” carrying familial and cultural memory across generations and borders.

item.title: «Iquo Ekong» / «Iquo Ubom» (Ibibio / Efik Odeon shellac pair)
item.description:
Background: # GM-NG-001 — «Iquo Ekong» / «Iquo Ubom» (Ibibio / Efik Odeon shellac pair)

Side a: «Iquo Ekong»

Side b: «Iquo Ubom»

item.title: Waring's Pennsylvanians, “Stack O'Lee Blues” (Victor 19189, 1923)
item.description: Background: The Stagolee ballad family preserves a violent grievance narrative, but this specific 1923 Waring recording is described by the historical sources as an instrumental fox trot. It has no verified sung text on which to assess accusation, retaliation, punishment or spite. The historical incident itself is a killing after a personal dispute, not automatically a revenge narrative. Under the project's core–narrative–context distinction, this recording is at most a context/version witness that shows how a Black American folk narrative entered mainstream dance-band recording. It should not be described as an audible revenge song or counted as a qualified new lead without further evidence and …

item.title: Caruso & Ruffo, "Sì, pel ciel marmoreo giuro!" (Verdi, *Otello*, Act II)
item.description:
Recording: Victor 89075, matrix C-14272-1, New York, 8 Jan 1914; Verdi (1813–1901), libretto Arrigo Boito (1842–1918)

Background: Otello and Iago kneel and swear vengeance on heaven at the end of Act II, the opera's central revenge oath.

Why it's here: an explicit vow of retaliation; pre-1926; composition and libretto long out of copyright.

item.title: Titta Ruffo, "Cortigiani, vil razza dannata" (Verdi, *Rigoletto*, Act II)
item.description:
Recording: Gramophone matrix 2735f, 24 Nov 1908, with La Scala orchestra, cond. Carlo Sabajno (US issue Victor 92066); Ruffo also re-recorded the aria later

Background: Rigoletto turns on the courtiers who abducted his daughter: public denunciation before the revenge plan.

Why it's here: accusation step of the revenge sequence in Vol. 2.

item.title: "Sì, vendetta" alternates: Galvany & Ruffo; Battistini & Hayes
item.description: Why it's here: same revenge duet as GM-IT-002; useful if the preferred Barrientos & Stracciari (Columbia 78363, 1919) transfer cannot be obtained.

item.title: Ma Rainey and her Georgia Band, "Stack O'Lee Blues"
item.description:
Recording: original Paramount 12357-A, New York, Dec 1925 (Jasper Taylor / Williams credit per Red Hot Jazz discography)

Background: the Stagolee killing told by the leading woman blues singer of the 1920s.

Why it's here: extends the Stagolee family in Vol. 3 with a Black woman's voice; pre-1926 recording.

item.title: Vernon Dalhart, "Jesse James" (Edison 51621)
item.description: Why it's here: third version of the "dirty little coward" accusation ballad.

item.title: Tuskegee Institute Singers, "I've Been 'Buked" (Victor, 1916)
item.description: Background: spiritual of endured insult ("I've been 'buked and I've been scorned").

item.title: Caruso & Scotti, "Ah Mimì, tu più non torni" (Puccini, *La Bohème*)
item.description: Fit: none (lament, not grievance). Keep only as excluded context, like GM-IT-001.

item.title: Julian Whiterose ("J. Resigna"), "Iron Duke in the Land" (Single Tone Calipso I), 1914
item.description:
Recording: Victor matrix G-145, Port of Spain, 11 Sep 1914, issued Victor 67362; also G-147 "Double Tone Calipso" ("Bayonet Charge by the Laws of Iron Duke"), Victor 67387

Background: among the first calypsos recorded with lyrics, sung in English by the leader of the White Rose Masquerade Band (real name Henry Julian).

Why it's here: calypso is public boast and insult (picong); a street-level, Caribbean form of the sung grudge, pre-1926.

item.title: Jules Sims, "Native Trinidad Kalenda" I–II, 1914
item.description:
Recording: Victor G-149/G-150, Port of Spain, 11 Sep 1914, with tamboo bamboo band

Background: kalenda are stick-fighting songs; tamboo bamboo bands played them on bamboo tubes after colonial authorities restricted skin drums (cite the ordinance before liner use).

Why it's here: music made with what the law left; fight songs.

item.title: Qamar-ol-Moluk Vaziri, 1924–25
item.description: Background: first concert at Tehran's Grand Hotel in 1924, the first public appearance of an Iranian woman singer before men without the veil. Featured on more than half of the 1925 sessions per the Honest Jon's compilation; later Polyphon 78s from 1927–28. One disc mourns the assassinated poet Mirzādeh Eshqi.

item.title: Ma Rainey, "Cell Bound Blues", 1924
item.description:
Recording: Paramount 12257-A, New York, 16 Oct 1924; composer Ma Rainey (d. 1939)

Background: sung in the voice of a woman jailed after a killing; the accused answers back.

item.title: The Plastic People of the Universe, *Egon Bondy's Happy Hearts Club Banned*
item.description: Background: recorded in secret at Houska Castle, Dec 1974, by a band banned from public performance; released only in France in 1978.

item.title: "Bone music" (roentgenizdat) X-ray records, late 1940s–early 1960s
item.description: Background: forbidden music cut onto used X-ray film. Sources: https://vice.com/en/article/soviet-russia-forbidden-music-x-ray-records · X-Ray Audio Project. Next: choose a disc whose source song is out of copyright.

item.title: cassettes from the 1982–91 Kurdish-language ban
item.description: Background: families hid tapes in their own language in gardens and charcoal stores. Sources: https://theatticmag.com/reports/2369/on-the-trails-of-a-banned-language.html

item.title: Radio Afghanistan (RTA) archive tapes hidden from the Taliban, 1996
item.description: Background: staff hid cassettes and claimed the archive had been looted; about 50,000 tapes survived. Sources: https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2005/11/13/saving-the-story-of-afghanistan · https://folkways.si.edu/magazine-summer-2011-afghanistans-collection/world-central-asia/music/article/smithsonian

item.title: SABC-barred records: Bernoldus Niemand "Snor City" (1988); Mzwakhe Mbuli "Change is Pain"
item.description: Background: SABC memos 273 (9 Feb 1989) and 322 (8 Nov 1990) barred them; censors scratched discs so they could not be aired. Sources: https://www.saha.org.za/shiftyrecords/sabc_internal_correspondence_restricted_records_memo_no_273.htm · https://www.saha.org.za/shiftyrecords/sabc_internal_correspondence_restricted_records_memo_no_322.htm · https://www.saha.org.za/radio_silence.htm

item.title: Thakhin movement, "Doh Bamar" (original 78, c.1930)
item.description: Background: a Rangoon collector says he holds the only original record of the song of the anti-colonial Dobama Asiayone ("We Burmans") movement, which later became the national anthem. Burmese labels pressed 78s from 1919 to 1962.

item.title: records banned under the 1933 Chōsen record-censorship rules (lead set)
item.description: Background: from 1933, the Government-General required lyrics and test pressings before sale; stampers were destroyed and issued discs confiscated. Mun Ok-bae's 일제의 노래검열 (Northeast Asian History Foundation, Dec 2025) lists banned titles; also Lee Jun-hee's SNU study (2007).

item.title: Taher Shah, "Eye to Eye" (2013) and "Angel" (2016)
item.description:
Background: written off as a joke and mocked on national TV in 2013, he came back in 2016 with "Angel". He left Pakistan in December 2016 after death threats.

Why it's here: the ridiculed maker who kept going. Frame with care: the threats are not a joke.

item.title: ARSCH, ARSCH
item.description:
Background: The artist's Bandcamp page identifies an 18-track ARSCH album released on 1 December 2020. It offers a limited cassette edition and digital album. The cassette uses professionally dubbed Type-I C-44 tapes, is hand-numbered, and has a different arrangement/mix from the digital edition. Tracks and durations are listed on the artist page: https://arsch.bandcamp.com/album/arsch

Where and when: Commune and barn studio, Bitsch, Valais, Switzerland; Date(s): Released Dec 2020 from earlier reels; Medium: Cassette / digital

Why it's here: Self-organised commune and barn-studio cassette/digital release; DIY communal life rather than a penal or medical institution.

item.description: Where and when: Kentucky State Penitentiary, Eddyville; Date(s): 1984; Medium: Cassette

item.title: Ernie Althoff's binaural cassettes, Clifton Hill Community Music Centre
item.description: Where and when: Melbourne, Australia; Date(s): 1976–83; Medium: Cassette

item.title: Mágicos do Som, two distinct Saúde Musical CDs (first c. 2000; second 2013)
item.description:
Background: Mágicos do Som is a music group associated with the CAPS Usina de Sonhos in Volta Redonda, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The 2007 UFF thesis by Raquel Siqueira da Silva documents the group's work in the mental-health service context and identifies Regina Lúcia Serrão as composer and singer of “Preconceito” (2000). The thesis reproduces a 1999 clipping showing that the CD was still being prepared, and a November 2000 clipping reporting a launch on the 22nd. The extracted copy does not make the exact event date fully unambiguous, so the first Saúde Musical CD is dated c. 2000, not assigned a precise day.

Where and when: CAPS Usina de Sonhos, Volta Redonda, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; Date(s): Group formed 1996; first CD c. 2000; second CD launched 13 Nov 2013; Medium: Two distinct CDs; first includes “Preconceito”; second has ten songs (six titles named in notice)

Why it's here: Brazilian CAPS community mental-health group; two separately documented CD objects, with group-authored songs.

item.title: Harmonia Enlouquece, selected album/track corpus
item.description:
Background: # IM-039 — Harmonia Enlouquece: fifth-album item-level reconciliation (2026-11-18)

Where and when: Centro Psiquiátrico Rio de Janeiro (CPRJ), Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; Date(s): 2001 onward; fifth album reported launched 2026-08-15; platform metadata 2026-07-05; Medium: CD / digital

Why it's here: Brazilian mixed user/professional group with a broad five-album catalogue; use as context rather than an obscurity claim.

item.title: Copacabana clandestine cassette compilation (“A FITA”), 17-track Latin American protest programme
item.description:
Background: # IM-043 — The Copacabana clandestine cassette compilation (“A FITA”), Rio de Janeiro, c.1975

Where and when: Concealed compartment in an apartment possibly used as a clandestine opposition safehouse; Copacabana, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; Date(s): Probably c.1975 (inferred from newest identified track); found 1984; Medium: 50 identical unbranded cassettes reported; one cassette later digitised to CD

item.title: Tardes Nuestras recurring opening theme (working incipit “Dicen que no tenemos razón”; official title unknown)
item.description:
Background: A 2017 Universidad Nacional de Rosario thesis records that the programme made contact with musicians and produced a song to serve as the cortina (opening/closing theme) of Tardes Nuestras. A 2020 La Capital article describes the recurring opening as a catchy rock song, quotes its opening lyric “Dicen que no tenemos razón,” and says that the song starts the programme. The station's official programme page links to its recorded-programme archive on RadioCut.

Where and when: CCGomecito / FM Aire Libre community radio, Rosario, Santa Fe, Argentina; Date(s): Programme created 2005; theme documented by 2017 and 2020; recording date unknown; Medium: Song embedded in recorded radio programmes; no standalone release identified; external musicians collaborated, resident authorship/performance unverified

item.title: Anões de Jardim, Demo
item.description:
Background: The band’s preserved Real Deal page says Anões de Jardim formed in January 1993, with Frederico P. Gomes, Felipe P. Gomes, Alexandre Velozo and Eurico Ludwig. It records the band’s first official performance at Curitiba’s 92 Degrees venue and says the first demo-tape was recorded live in Studio Solo in July 1993, with eight songs and weak distribution in the independent market.

Where and when: Independent hardcore/DIY cassette scene, Curitiba, Paraná, Brazil; Date(s): July 1993; Medium: Eight-track demo cassette; collector-reported digitised copy
